slides.title: Chapter 19: Keeping Time, Scheduling Tasks, and Launching Programs
slides.say: Chapter 18 worked with files that programs read and write. Chapter 19 turns to time and to other programs: how a program reads a clock, waits, writes and reads dates, and how it starts, stops and schedules another program. This deck follows the chapter in its own order: the time module with the epoch timestamp and sleep and Project 14, the Super Stopwatch; the datetime module with moments, durations, strftime() and strptime(); launching programs with subprocess.run() and subprocess.Popen(), the start and open commands and the scheduler paragraph; and Project 15, the Simple Countdown, with the two practice programs. It adds what the chapter leaves out and what the research found when every printed output was run again: four en dashes that make listings a SyntaxError, a profiling listing that does not match the file the book ships, a time zone named Pacific Standard Time on a day when it was Pacific Daylight Time, a two-digit year that maps 69 to 1969, thirty years that are seven days short, time zones and daylight saving, the utcnow() deprecation, the commands of Windows and macOS that Linux lacks, and what real cron did on a real machine. Everything printed on these slides was produced by Python 3.14.6, installed with uv, with tzdata 2026.5 and schedule 1.2.2; time, datetime, zoneinfo and subprocess are the standard library. Nothing on a slide depends on the time of day: every moment is built from numbers, every zone is named, and the stopwatch and countdown run on a clock the program moves. What could not be run, a Windows computer, a Mac, a systemd timer, a sound card and the final release of Python 3.15, is marked NOT EXECUTED on its slide.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: The route has six parts. It starts with clocks: the epoch timestamp and the choice of an engineer in the story of the epoch, the clock that answers each question, sleeping and the drift of a loop, Project 14, the Super Stopwatch, and the repairs the listings need before they run. Then dates and text: what a program can do with datetime, durations in a timedelta, strftime() with Table 19-1 and strptime() with its two-digit year. Then time zones: naive and aware values, the zone of the chapter's example, and the 23-hour day, the gap and the fold of daylight saving. Then launching programs: run() and Popen(), poll, wait, the check and the timeout, exit codes and signals, and the shell with the commands start and open that Linux lacks. The fifth part is scheduling and the practice programs: Timer, sched and call_later inside a process, cron fields and what real cron did, Project 15 with the Prettified Stopwatch, and the Friday the 13th finder. The last part is a one-map summary and the resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need. Two of the slides are true stories and four more are told in the notes; the eight narrative diagrams of the chapter are drawn from the same specifications as the interactive page. Every output was printed by Python 3.14.6 with tzdata 2026.5 and schedule 1.2.2, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: The first question is the spine of the chapter. A program can read several clocks, and they answer different questions: time.time() answers what moment is it, time.monotonic() answers how long did this take. A datetime holds a moment and a timedelta a duration, and both refuse or misread things: a timedelta has no months, a two-digit year maps 69 to 1969, a value with no zone cannot be compared with one that has a zone, and a day added across a daylight saving change is 23 hours long. A program launches another program with a list of arguments through subprocess.run(), which waits, or subprocess.Popen(), which does not, and it schedules a program either inside a process that stays alive or with the operating system, where the commands of the book, start and open, may not exist. The second question is the watch-out of the deck. The chapter page of 13 October 2026 has 29 listings, 20 of them interactive sessions of 75 statements, one figure and one table. All 75 statements were replayed in order under Python 3.14.6 with the zone of the author, America/Los_Angeles: 54 printed what the book prints and 21 did not, of which 7 depend on the clock, 1 is the en dash and 13 launch Windows or macOS programs or call a program that Linux lacks; with the dash repaired 55 matched. The online materials of the book, 91 files, hold three files of this chapter, calcProd.py, stopwatch.py and simplecountdown.py, and none of the alarm.wav, the hello.txt or the practice programs. Each slide says where a printed line differs and on what evidence.

slides.title: The epoch timestamp
slides.say: The chapter says the epoch timestamp is the number of seconds since the epoch, a reference moment that many date and time programs use, and that the moment is January 1, 1970, UTC. The program shows what that definition leaves out. calendar.timegm() turns a moment in UTC into its timestamp, so the moment 06:04:35 on 18 March 2026 is 1773813875, the whole-second part of the chapter's example; timestamp 0 is the first moment of 1970. The POSIX formula that defines the number gives every day exactly 86,400 seconds, so the leap second of 31 December 2016 has no number: the two seconds on either side of it are one second apart in epoch time, and datetime refuses a 60th second. A float has limited precision: near the chapter's timestamp neighbouring floats are about 2.4e-07 apart, a quarter of a microsecond. The last lines show the year 2038 problem: a signed 32-bit count of seconds reaches 2**31 - 1 at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038, and the next second, packed into 32 bits and read back as signed, is -2147483648, which is 20:45:52 UTC on 13 December 1901. Python on a 64-bit machine is not affected, but file formats and old C programs may be. The chapter does not mention leap seconds or 2038; Appendix B's answer to question 1 names the same moment, January 1, 1970, UTC.

slides.title: An epoch chosen by engineers
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on Unix time cites the first edition of the Unix Programmer's Manual, dated 3 November 1971, which says time returns the time since 00:00:00, Jan. 1, 1971, measured in sixtieths of a second. The third edition, dated 15 March 1972, counts from Jan. 1, 1972, and adds that the time is stored in 32 bits, which guarantees a crisis every 2.26 years. Counting sixtieths of a second in 32 bits runs out after 2**32 / 60 seconds, which is 2.27 years by this study's arithmetic. The article says the current epoch of 1 January 1970 was selected arbitrarily by Unix engineers because it was a convenient date to work with, and the precision was changed to seconds to avoid short-term overflow. In this study time.gmtime(0) gave 1970-01-01 00:00:00 and calendar.timegm of that moment gave 0. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Unix time' (the epoch selected arbitrarily; the manual of 3 November 1971 with the epoch of 1971; the manual of 15 March 1972 with the epoch of 1972 and 2.26 years), read 2026-10-13; this study's leaves EpochZero and FloatPrecision. The console on the slide runs the arithmetic of the story: time.gmtime(0) is the first moment of 1970 and calendar.timegm of it is 0, the largest signed 32-bit count is 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038, and 2**32 sixtieths of a second last 2.27 years by this deck's arithmetic, close to the 2.26 the manual states.

slides.title: Which clock answers which question
slides.say: The chapter times code by subtracting two readings of time.time(), and Project 14 does the same for laps. get_clock_info() says what each clock is. time.time() reads CLOCK_REALTIME, which is the system clock: monotonic False, adjustable True, so an administrator or a time service can set it, and then a difference can be negative. monotonic() and perf_counter() read CLOCK_MONOTONIC, which cannot go backwards and cannot be adjusted; the Python documentation and PEP 418 name them for intervals. process_time() reads the CPU time of this process, so it does not run while the program sleeps. The program cannot set the real clock back, so it says EMULATED: two numbers stand in, the wall clock 1000.0 then 990.0 and the monotonic clock 50.0 then 60.0, and the difference is -10.0 on the first and +10.0 on the second. The last line measures a sleep on the monotonic clock and compares it with a bound, so the line prints the same on every run. For an exact interval the course therefore uses monotonic() or perf_counter(), and keeps time() for a moment on a calendar.

slides.title: Pausing: sleep, polling and drift
slides.say: The activity diagram is the chapter's way of pausing a program until a date: make a datetime for the date, read the current moment, and while the moment is earlier than the date pause with time.sleep(1) and read it again, then continue. The one-second sleep is what keeps the loop from using the processor all the time; the research measured it once: the loop with the sleep used under 0.05 of processor time in 1.2 of elapsed time, and the loop without it over 0.1 in 0.3. The program shows four things the chapter does not say. time.sleep() returns None and lasts at least the time asked, measured on the monotonic clock. Since Python 3.5 a signal handler that returns does not shorten the sleep, which is retried for the time that remains, as PEP 475 says: the handler ran and the sleep still lasted at least 0.3. A loop that sleeps one second after its work drifts: with 0.02 of work in each round, the 3600th round starts at 3670.98, which is 71.98 late, while a loop anchored to the tick starts it at 3599.0 as it should. And round() goes to the even neighbour on a tie, so round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4, and it returns an int without a digits argument; round(2.675, 2) is 2.67 because the float is a little below 2.675. Appendix B answers question 5 with the closest integer, which is incomplete for exactly this reason.

slides.title: Project 14: the Super Stopwatch
slides.say: The activity diagram is the chapter's program, step by step: note the start time with time.time(), wait for ENTER, subtract the last time to get the lap time, round the lap time and the total time to two digits, print the lap number, the total time and the lap time, and ask whether the user pressed Ctrl-C. The real program needs a terminal, because it calls input(); run without one it raises EOFError at the first call. So the program on the slide says EMULATED: it adds the gaps 3.56, 5.07, 9.05 and 1.43 to a fake clock instead of waiting for a person, and prints the laps the chapter prints, 3.56 and 3.56, 8.63 and 5.07, 17.68 and 9.05, 19.11 and 1.43. The last line shows a trap of the shipped file: stopwatch.py in the online materials has no f prefix on its print, so it prints the braces, Lap #{lap_number}: {total_time}({lap_time}), where the chapter's listing has the prefix; the shipped file also has two en dashes, which the next slide explains. The chapter prints the total time and the lap time without a space between them, while the Prettified Stopwatch practice program, on a later slide, pads them into columns with rjust().

slides.title: What the listings need before they run
slides.say: The chapter's listings, as served on its web page, need repairs before they run. Four places in three listings, listings 2, 6 and 12, write the en dash U+2013 instead of the minus sign, in end_time – start_time, time.time() – last_time and oct_21st – about_thirty_years. The first console rows show the refusal, SyntaxError: invalid character '–' (U+2013), and the same expression with a minus sign. A reader who copies the listing gets a program that does not start. The shipped files are another matter: calcProd.py in the online materials is not the program the chapter prints. It loops over range(1, 100000), prints len(str(result)) and has an en dash; repaired, it raises ValueError because Python refuses to convert an integer of more than 4300 digits to a string by default, which the console shows with str(math.factorial(100000)). The number of digits of 100000! is 456574, computed here without converting it. The timings are single runs of the research on one machine: the product took about 2.3 to 2.6 seconds and math.factorial(100000), which gives the same integer, 0.136 seconds, and they vary with the machine. The chapter prints 2.844162940979004 seconds for its own run. The shipped stopwatch.py also has CRLF line ends, two en dashes and no f prefix on its print, which the previous slide showed.

slides.title: What a program can do with datetime
slides.say: The use-case diagram lists what the chapter does with moments and durations through one module: make a moment from a year, month and day, read the current moment, compare two moments, add a duration to a moment, turn a moment into text with strftime() and read text into a moment with strptime(). They are independent uses of the same module and not a sequence, which is why the picture is a set of uses. The seventh, attaching a time zone with ZoneInfo, is not in the chapter. The console builds the moments from numbers: Halloween 2026 is earlier than 1 January 2027, their difference is the timedelta of 62 days, 31 October 2026 is a weekday numbered 5, a Saturday, and a day that does not exist, 30 February, raises ValueError. The last row is Appendix B's answer to question 7: the weekday() of 7 January 2019 is 0, Monday. datetime.now() would print the moment the slide was run, so no row calls it; the research recorded the chapter's own statements of that kind, and they differ from the book's because they come from four different days in the book (11:05 on 17 March 2026, 27 February 2026, 21 October 2026 and 2 December 2026). Python 3.12 deprecated utcnow() for now(datetime.UTC), which a later slide shows.

slides.title: Durations: timedelta
slides.say: A timedelta stores a duration as days, seconds and microseconds. The chapter's example, 11 days, 10 hours, 9 minutes and 8 seconds, has days 11, seconds 36548 and total_seconds() 986948.0, and prints as 11 days, 10:09:08. It has no months or years, because they are not fixed lengths: months=1 raised TypeError, with the message of Python 3.14, which differs in 3.11, 3.12 and 3.15, as the research found by running eleven interpreters. Adding 30 days to 31 January gives 2 March and adding 31 gives 3 March, so there is no single addition that means a month. The chapter's about_thirty_years is 365 * 30 days and the chapter says it ignores leap years, but it prints 28 October 1996 for 30 years before 21 October 2026, which is 7 days off because the span holds 7 leap days; twice the span prints 5 November 1966, 15 days off. The text before the example calls the function datetime.delta(), which raises AttributeError: module 'datetime' has no attribute 'delta'; the function is datetime.timedelta(). For a real calendar span use replace(year=...), as the program does, or a library.

slides.title: strftime: a moment to text
slides.say: Table 19-1 of the chapter lists the directives of strftime(). The table on the slide is computed, not typed: for each directive it calls strftime() on the moment 16:29:07 on 3 November 2026, a Tuesday, so %w, the weekday with Sunday as 0, prints 2 and %j, the day of the year, prints 307. The names of days and months come from the C locale. The chapter sends the reader to strftime.org for the directives; that address now redirects with HTTP 301 to a cheatsheet of another company, which the links check of this deck does not count on. The program writes the chapter's year/month/day format, a 12-hour clock with %p, the weekday and month names, and a literal percent sign written as %%. It then shows the form the course recommends for storing a moment, ISO 8601: isoformat() writes 2026-11-03T16:29:07, timespec='minutes' shortens it, an aware value ends in +00:00, and fromisoformat() reads it back, since Python 3.11 including the letter Z and the week form 2026-W43-3, a Wednesday. The chapter mentions neither isoformat() nor ISO 8601, and the internet standard for timestamps is RFC 3339.

slides.title: strptime: text to a moment
slides.say: strptime() is the inverse of strftime(): the format must describe the text exactly. October 21, 2026 with %B %d, %Y is a moment at midnight. The chapter's example uses November of '63 and '73, and the table of this slide computes the rule for %y: Table 19-1 says 00 to 99 means 1970 to 2069, but Python and POSIX map 69 to 99 to 1969 to 1999 and 00 to 68 to 2000 to 2068, so '68' is 2068 and '69' is 1969; the book's two examples, 63 as 2063 and 73 as 1973, are right either way. A text that does not match raises ValueError and names the text and the format, as the second part of the transcript shows; %B wants the full month name and refuses Oct. A date with no year gets the year 1900, which draws a DeprecationWarning since Python 3.13 for 29 February, since 1900 was not a leap year. Python 3.15.0b4, the only 3.15 the research could install, raises ValueError for %d without a year; Python 3.15.0 final, released on 9 October 2026 by python.org's list, and Python 3.14.7 and later were NOT EXECUTED, because uv offered only 3.14.6 and 3.15.0b4 on the day. Python 3.14 added date.strptime() and time.strptime(), which the last line uses.

slides.title: Time zones: naive and aware
slides.say: A naive datetime has no zone and an aware one has; comparing them for equality gives False and subtracting them raises TypeError. The chapter has no time zone object, so the program uses zoneinfo, in the standard library since Python 3.9 (PEP 615): 16:29 UTC is equal to 19:29 in Istanbul. The chapter's moment, 1773813875.35, is 23:04:35 on 17 March 2026 in Los Angeles, and the zone name is PDT: the chapter says Pacific Standard Time, but daylight saving time began in the United States on 8 March 2026, so the zone was Pacific Daylight Time at -07:00, and the printed ctime of 11:05:38 reads 23:05 on a 24-hour clock. The same second, 1,000,000, is 05:46:40 in Los Angeles, 13:46:40 in UTC and 15:46:40 in Istanbul, so the chapter's fromtimestamp(1000000) is right only in the author's zone; Istanbul was UTC+02:00 in January 1970 and UTC+03:00 in July 2026, as the last line prints, so the offset of a zone depends on the date. zoneinfo reads the operating system's tz database or the tzdata package and raises ZoneInfoNotFoundError with neither; in the bare environment of the research, with no tzdata package, zoneinfo still worked from the system's data. The story of the database, a lawsuit that shut down its mailing list for a week in October 2011 until ICANN took it over, is in the notes of the resources slide. This is a record of 13 October 2026 on an Ubuntu 24.04 machine whose system tz database is 2026c.

slides.title: Daylight saving: 23 hours, a gap, a fold
slides.say: Noon on 7 March 2026 in New York plus one day is noon on 8 March, and between them the clocks went forward: the difference in UTC is 23 hours while the wall-clock difference is 1 day, because a timedelta added to an aware datetime moves the wall clock. The hour from 02:00 to 03:00 on 8 March does not exist: asking for 02:30 there and converting to UTC and back gives 03:30. The hour from 01:00 to 02:00 on 1 November happens twice, and the attribute fold, added by PEP 495, tells the two apart: 01:30 with fold 0 is 05:30 UTC and with fold 1 is 06:30 UTC, although the two values compare equal. The chapter has none of this. The last two lines are about a deprecation: Python 3.12 deprecated datetime.utcnow() and utcfromtimestamp(), which return naive values in UTC, in favour of now(datetime.UTC), which returns an aware value; the program catches the DeprecationWarning and prints its category. The Python documentation lists datetime.UTC, added in Python 3.11, as an alias of timezone.utc. The research ran the same lines under eleven interpreters, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, the seven 3.14 releases and 3.15.0b4: 11 of 48 compared items differ between releases, among them this deprecation, the error text of sleep('1'), and the text of the error for timedelta(months=1).

slides.title: Launching a program: run() or Popen()
slides.say: The flow chart is the choice the chapter walks through: put the program and its arguments in a list of strings, then decide whether the program should wait for the process to end. If it should, call subprocess.run() with the list, pass capture_output=True and text=True to get the output, and check=True and a timeout to raise on a failure; if it should not, call subprocess.Popen() and use poll(), which returns None while the process runs. The program runs both on this machine. run(['sleep', '0.3']) returned a CompletedProcess with returncode 0 after the child ended. With capture_output=True the output is bytes, b'out\n' and b'err\n', and the child's standard error is captured separately; with text=True the same output is a str. Popen returned at once: poll() gave None while the child slept, then wait() blocked and returned 0, and poll() gave 0. The chapter opens the calculator six times with Popen on Windows, and Figure 19-1 is a screenshot of the six windows; calc.exe, notepad and mspaint were NOT EXECUTED, because the machine is Linux, and the picture is not reproduced here. The alt text of the opening picture of the chapter is empty and the alt text of Figure 19-1 describes a Windows desktop with six overlapping calculator programs.

slides.title: Popen: poll, wait, check, timeout
slides.say: The sequence diagram follows the exchange between the program, the Popen object and the process: the program calls Popen() with a list, the object starts the process and returns at once, poll() returns None while the process runs, wait() blocks until the process ends with an exit code, and the object returns the code. The program on the slide shows what the chapter does not. check=True turns a non-zero exit status into CalledProcessError: false exits 1, and the message says so. A timeout turns a program that hangs into TimeoutExpired, and run() kills the child before it raises; the message names the command and the time, and its wording of the time depends on the release, which the research found by running eleven interpreters. A program that does not exist raises FileNotFoundError, not a non-zero exit code. The last lines show that a list passes the arguments untouched: 'my file.txt' stays one argument, and '*.txt' is not expanded, because no shell is involved. That is the reason to prefer a list over a string for a program you know. The chapter's example passes the name of a file to notepad on Windows as the second item of the list; that program was NOT EXECUTED here.

slides.title: A process from start to exit
slides.say: The state diagram follows a launched process: Popen starts it, it runs while poll() gives None, and it ends either with an exit code or by a signal. The program runs five children and prints their return codes: a program that does nothing returns 0, sys.exit(3) returns 3, an uncaught exception returns 1, and a child that was killed by SIGKILL has the return code -9 and one ended by SIGTERM -15, the negative of the signal number. The corpus program of the research ran the rest: sys.exit('msg') also returns 1, os._exit(256 + 7) returns 7 because an exit status holds eight bits, terminate() on a child with a SIGTERM handler printed asked to stop, saving work and returned 0, kill() returned -9 and printed nothing, and trying to handle SIGKILL raised OSError with errno 22. The chapter mentions none of this; it has no exit codes, no terminate() and no kill(). A timeout in run() kills the child with SIGKILL, which is the last transition of the diagram. On Windows the same words exist, terminate() and kill() both call TerminateProcess, but Windows was NOT EXECUTED, so the slide claims nothing about it.

slides.title: The shell, and opening files
slides.say: The chapter opens a file with the default application by running start on Windows and open on macOS and Linux. The program asks what a Linux machine does. A list with shell=True runs only its first item: echo ran with no arguments and printed an empty line, and the second item became the zero argument of the shell, which is why the failing start printed hello.txt: 1: start: not found and returned 127. A string with shell=True works. A command built from a file name is the danger: the file name x; echo INJECTED ran a second command, shlex.quote() prevented it, and so did a list with no shell. open exists here as /usr/bin/open only because the xdg-utils package registers it as an alternative of xdg-open; start does not exist, and os.startfile, the Windows way, is absent. webbrowser.open() returned False with no browser to open, and pyperclip, which the chapter introduces in Chapter 8, raised an error with no clipboard program. All of the following were NOT EXECUTED: the commands of Windows and macOS, and any program that needs a desktop. The research ran xdg-open on a file that did not exist, which exited 2 and said so, and that is all it can say about it here.

slides.title: Running a job later
slides.say: The use-case diagram lists what a program can do to run a job later: write a cron entry with five time fields, call a function once after a delay with Timer, order events by time and priority with sched, call a function later with asyncio's call_later, run jobs every day with the schedule package, describe a job in a launchd property list, and normalise a systemd calendar expression. The chapter gives the operating system schedulers one paragraph, Task Scheduler, launchd and cron, and its Summary points to the book's page at No Starch Press for instructions that the page does not hold. The program runs the three that live inside a process. sched ran its events in order of time and then priority on a clock the program moves, so it says EMULATED: now at 0, two at 2, five first at 5 with priority 0 and five at 5 with priority 1, and the clock ended at 5.0. threading.Timer returns at once, so the list was still empty after start() and held fired after join(). call_later ran soon first, then the 0.1 callback, then the 0.2 one. The schedule package, version 1.2.2, the newest release on 13 October 2026, uploaded on 25 May 2024, computed its first run at 10:30 for a job set every day at that time; in a Python with only the standard library, importing it raised ModuleNotFoundError. All four need a process that stays alive; if the machine restarts, they are gone, which is the reason for an operating system scheduler.

slides.title: Cron: five fields and a small world
slides.say: A crontab line has five time fields, minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week, and then the command. The matcher on the slide is the study's own function, written to the rule of the Debian manual page. The manual page says that when both day fields are restricted a command runs when either matches, so 0 0 13 * 5 is not Friday the 13th: it fires on every 13th and on every Friday, and the next run after 9:30 on Tuesday 13 October 2026 is the Friday 16 October. The other lines show 9:30 on weekdays, every 15 minutes, and 29 February, which waits until 2028. The research then ran cron for real on this machine, cron 3.0pl1-184 on Ubuntu 24.04, and these are records of 13 October 2026, not results the deck recomputes. A Python job started by cron two seconds after the turn of the minute saw PATH=/usr/bin:/bin, the working directory /root, no terminal and sh as its parent, and its local clock read 22:36:01 UTC while the shell showed 01:36:01 +03. A TZ=Asia/Kolkata line in the crontab reached the job and set its clock to IST; a minute of 61 was refused by crontab with exit code 1 and the message bad minute. The schedule follows the zone of the cron daemon: started from a shell whose TZ was Europe/Istanbul, an entry written on the Istanbul clock fired at the target moment and the entry for the same moment on the UTC clock did not, while a CRON_TZ=Asia/Kolkata line was passed to the job as a variable but did not move the schedule, and the Debian manual page does not mention CRON_TZ. Task Scheduler, launchd and a systemd timer were NOT EXECUTED: a launchd property list for 04:00 daily was written and read back with plistlib, 501 bytes and equal, and systemd-analyze only normalised Mon..Fri 09:00 to Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00:00. Wikipedia's article on cron says the cron of Version 7 Unix was a daemon that read its crontab, ran the commands due at that minute as root, slept for one minute and repeated. It was robust but consumed resources whether or not there was work, and an experiment at Purdue University in the late 1970s to give cron's service to all 100 users of a time-shared VAX put too much load on the system. A Purdue graduate student, Robert Brown, recognised the parallel between cron and discrete event simulators after reading the article of Franta and Maly and built an event-list implementation. On this study's machine cron 3.0pl1 started a Python job at the turn of a minute with PATH=/usr/bin:/bin, the working directory /root and no terminal. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Cron' (Version 7 algorithm; Purdue in the late 1970s; Robert Brown and the Franta-Maly event list manager), read 2026-10-13; this study's real cron run (live record) and leaves CronFields and CronEnvironment.

slides.title: Project 15 and the Prettified Stopwatch
slides.say: Project 15, the Simple Countdown, counts down from 60 with time.sleep(1) between the numbers and then plays a sound file with playsound3. The loop on the slide is the same loop with 5 in place of 60, and it says EMULATED: a number that the loop increases stands in for the clock that time.sleep(1) would move, so it prints 5 4 3 2 1 and counts 5.0 seconds of fake time without waiting. The sound was NOT EXECUTED: the machine has no sound card, the online materials do not hold alarm.wav, and autbor.com/alarm.wav redirects with HTTP 302 to a file of 582,952 bytes and 3.30 seconds on the book's own site. The shipped simplecountdown.py matches the printed listing apart from spacing, but the copy served at autbor.com differs: it sets timeLeft to 2, uses camel case and has the Windows start line uncommented. Appendix A pins playsound3 2.4.0; the newest release on 13 October 2026 is 3.3.2, uploaded on 18 July 2026, and the pins environment of the research holds 2.4.0. The second program is the first practice program, the Prettified Stopwatch: rjust() pads the lap number to 2, and the times to 6, so the columns line up, where the chapter's Project 14 printed them without padding. The numbers come from the laps of the stopwatch slide.

slides.title: Friday the 13th, forward and backward
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on the Gregorian calendar says it was instituted by the papal bull Inter gravissimas dated 24 February 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII, after whom it is named. To bring Easter back to the season of its introduction the reform advanced the date by 10 days, so Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October 1582. The Python documentation calls date an idealized naive date, assuming the current Gregorian calendar always was, and always will be, in effect. In this study date(1582, 10, 5) existed and was a Tuesday, and date(1582, 10, 15) was a Friday, as in the history. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Gregorian calendar' (the bull of 24 February 1582; Thursday 4 October 1582 followed by Friday 15 October 1582), read 2026-10-13; Python 3.14 documentation of datetime; this study's leaves GregorianCalendar and WeekdayOfDate. The second practice program of the chapter finds the next ten Friday the 13ths from a date. From a fixed day, 13 October 2026, the first is 13 November 2026 and the tenth 13 August 2032. The research also walked backward day by day until Python stopped it: 3,485 such dates down to 13 April of the year 1, and then OverflowError: date value out of range at 1 January of the year 1. The chart is computed: over 400 years from 2000, the 13th falls on a Friday 688 times, the most of any weekday, and on a Thursday 684 times, because the Gregorian calendar repeats every 146,097 days, which is exactly 20,871 weeks. Every year from 1 to 9999 has at least one Friday the 13th, which the corpus program of the research checked. The chapter's two practice programs are not in the online materials: the zip holds no prettifiedStopwatch.py and no fridayThirteenth.py, so this deck's programs are written from the chapter's description.

slides.title: The chapter in one map
slides.say: These six branches are the route of the deck. The epoch and the clock: the epoch is 1970 in UTC, a monotonic clock gives the true difference, and sleep waits at least the time asked. The datetime module: a timedelta has no months, a two-digit year maps 69 to 1969, and a date with no year uses 1900. Time zones: a naive value has no zone, a day across the change is 23 hours, and a signed 32-bit count ends in 2038. Launching programs: run() waits and Popen does not, a list of arguments passes through no shell, and start and open are not on Linux. Scheduling: cron has five time fields, a cron job does not run in your shell, and sched and Timer run inside a Python process. The last branch is the book and its practice: four places write an en dash, the stopwatch prints the laps, and the 13th is a Friday 688 times in 400 years. Together they answer the first question of the chapter, which clock, which moment and which launcher answers each question, and the slides that say where a printed line differs answer the second. The map is drawn from the same specification as the interactive page.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Every link on this slide was opened on the day the deck was made, and the build records the status each answered. The textbook chapter is free to read online and holds every listing of the chapter; the documentation of the time, datetime, zoneinfo, subprocess and sched modules describes them. The reference links are the pages for the topics where the deck corrected or extended the chapter: the POSIX definition of seconds since the epoch, and the manual page of crontab that states the rule for the two day fields. The history links are the sources behind the six stories of the chapter. Two of them are slides, the epoch chosen by Unix engineers and the Gregorian calendar; the other four are told in the notes: the leap second and the year 2038 on the slide of the epoch timestamp, the lawsuit that shut down the time zone database's mailing list on the slide of time zones, and cron at Purdue on the slide of cron. The tzdata and schedule packages are the two third-party packages whose versions the deck records. The rest of the sixty-odd sources of the research, among them the PEPs, the RFCs and the manual pages of launchd and systemd, are in the research package.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.say: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed. If you can say them in your own words and run the examples yourself, you have the chapter. The console rows use only numbers and named zones, so they can be typed into any Python and give the same text on any day; time, datetime, calendar, zoneinfo and subprocess are the standard library, and the programs build their own files in a temporary folder and use no network. The rows were run again under Python 3.14.6 with tzdata 2026.5 each time the deck was built, and the programs were run again by the check that compares the slides with the recording. What was not run is marked on its slide: a Windows computer, a Mac, a systemd timer, a sound card, and the final release of Python 3.15 with Python 3.14.7 and later. The next chapter of the book sends email, texts and push notifications, and what this chapter taught about launching and scheduling programs, and about the difference between a moment and an interval, carries over.
